title: The prince and his gurus
hookLine: Ganga names the teachers her son learned from, starting with the sage who cursed him: why Hindus honor the guru
carry: knowledge comes down from guru to student
last: GANGA IS A MOTHER, NOT JUST A RIVER.

cards: Rama, the son of Jamadagni. That's the list Ganga gives the king.

She's standing before Shantanu at the river's edge, holding their grown son by the hand, and before she lets go of him she tells his father what the boy has learned while he was away, and whose learning he holds.
It's an extraordinary list. And the first name on it should make us stop.

teach.h: TAUGHT BY THE SAGE WHO CURSED HIM.
teach.b: He studied the Vedas, Ganga says, with Vasishtha. That's the sage whose cow was stolen, who cursed the Vasus, and who said the one who took her would live long on earth. The one who took her was Dyu.
And Dyu is this young man. So the sage who sentenced him to a human life is the one who taught him how to live it.

teach.h: THE TEACHERS OF GODS AND ASURAS.
teach.b: He knows everything Ushanas knows, the teacher the asuras follow, and everything Brihaspati knows, the teacher of the gods.
And he knows every weapon known to Rama, the son of Jamadagni, the warrior sage tradition calls Parashurama. Take him home, she says, and she goes back into the water.
Shantanu brings his son to the capital and makes him heir, and the text says the people are glad of him. Notice how Ganga shows the king his son is ready. By naming his teachers.
That's one of the oldest ideas in Hinduism: real knowledge isn't something you pick up alone.
It comes down from guru to shishya, teacher to student, in an unbroken line called a parampara. Who taught you is part of what you know.
That's why students of Indian music and dance still touch their teacher's feet before a lesson, and why many Hindus keep Guru Purnima, a full-moon day for honoring teachers.

teach.h: KNOWLEDGE COMES DOWN FROM GURU TO STUDENT.
teach.b: It's also called Vyasa Purnima, after Vyasa, the sage tradition says composed this very poem. One Vasu stays on earth, carrying the learning of gods and asuras, taught by the sage who cursed him.

practice: Many Hindu prayers begin by remembering the guru. Bring to mind a teacher you honor: a guru, a parent, whoever first taught you your faith or your craft. If it's your way, bow your head or touch the ground before you.

Breathe in and feel what they gave you; breathe out and let a quiet thank you go to them. If you don't pray, simply trace one thing you know back to the person who taught it, and thank them in your heart.
